A B S T R A C T
Intelligent shipping systems advance deep learning applications in ship trajectory prediction, enhancing maritime 
security risk identification. However, existing models struggle to capture multi-ship interactions in high-density 
areas due to the significant influence of neighboring vessels. To address this, we propose a trajectory prediction 
method integrating Kullback-Leibler divergence attention (KLDA) and a dual-stream parallel architecture. First, a 
transposition interactive convolutional network (TICNet) employs a dual-layer convolution structure to model dy­
namic interactions between target and adjacent ships. Second, KLDA mitigates amplitude interference by mapping 
feature vectors to probability distributions, decoupling similarity computation from input amplitude to suppress 
dominant local outliers in attention maps. Third, the time-feature dual-stream strategy separately models tem­
poral dependencies via time-embedding sequences and encodes heterogeneous features as tokens using sample 
transposition, with self-attention explicitly capturing feature correlations. Finally, a cascaded transformer de­
coder (CTD) iteratively refines outputs through recursive optimization. Experimental results on three real-world 
scenarios demonstrate average displacement error reductions of 16.75%, 33.48%, and 45.63% compared to the 
best baseline, validating the method’s effectiveness in complex, high-density navigation environments.

Introduction Global trade is driving the shipping industry’s intelligent transfor­ mation. A key feature of this shift is the deep integration of artificial intelligence, sensing, and communication technologies [ 1 ]. As a critical infrastructure for sensing ship dynamics, the automatic identification system (AIS) continuously broadcasts real-time status data, including position, speed, and heading, via radio waves, thereby providing foun­ dational data support for research in ship trajectory prediction [ 2 ] and trajectory completion [ 3 ]. It fuses historical trajectory data with real-time operational status to achieve high-precision estimation of fu­ ture ship positions [ 4 ]. This supports multiple objectives: improving energy efficiency, reducing emissions, enabling autonomous control, and preventing collisions. More broadly, it advances the entire maritime system toward a data-driven intelligent paradigm. Despite significant progress in ship trajectory prediction in recent years, existing methods still face three key limitations. First, insufficient targeted modeling capability. Traditional methods rely on kinematic method [ 5 ] to describe the nonlinearity and uncertainty of ship mo­ tion [ 6 ]. Attention mechanism-based trajectory prediction models Deep learning methods leverage deep architectures and multilayer neural networks to learn and model input data, enabling robust learn­ ing capabilities and adaptability. These models demonstrate excep­ tional performance in processing complex and dynamic trajectory data. The attention mechanism, central to the Transformer architecture, has emerged as a dominant paradigm in sequential modeling due to its abil­ ity to capture long-range dependencies, parallel computation efficiency, and dynamic weight allocation. Unlike traditional recurrent networks, which suffer from gradient vanishing and limited scalability, attention mechanisms enable global interactions and adaptive feature weight­ ing, making them superior for complex tasks. For instance, Capobianco et al. [ 52 ] proposed the encoder-decoder based on the attention frame­ work (ED-ATTN), which integrates attention mechanisms with RNNs to learn spatiotemporal correlations from historical ship data for trajectory prediction. The transformer architecture, built on self-attention mechanisms, has become a cornerstone in time series forecasting due to its paral­ lelizable computation and strong sequence modeling capabilities [ 44 ]. Xue et al. [ 45 ] combined Transformer with GRU (G-Trans), where GRU captures temporal features while the Transformer addresses long-term trajectory sequence correlations. Huang et al. [ 56 ] adapted the PatchTST framework to maritime applications by partitioning long sequences into fixed-length patches for localized pattern recognition. Lin et al. [ 46 ] introduced the HDFormer model, which employs trajectory and environmental attention modules to integrate spatial features from his­ torical trajectories and hydrological fields. However, transformer-based methods remain limited in explicitly modeling multi-ship interactions, highlighting a critical challenge in collaborative trajectory prediction. CNNs excel in feature extraction and spatial interaction fusion, partic­ ularly for capturing spatial patterns in ship navigation data. Ma et al. [ 59 ] proposed an LSTM model with multi-scale convolution and atten­ tion (LMCA) to better capture ship dynamics. Yuan et al. [ 57 ] proposed a hybrid TCN-Transformer model, combining the temporal convolu­ tional network (TCN) with Transformer to enhance interaction modeling in time series. Syed et al. Dual-stream parallel encoder (DSPE) The proposed dual-stream parallel encoder is designed based on a parallel time-feature dual-stream architecture. On one hand, it models ship navigation states across temporal steps and cross-feature interac­ tion dependencies through the TICN module. Transposition interactive convolutional network (TICN) After extracting the navigation status information of the target ship and the surrounding adjacent ships. Inspired by the interactive convo­ lutional blocks proposed by Eldele et al. [ 21 ], we designed a trajectory interaction convolution network for extracting trajectory interaction in­ formation. Based on the feature stream data, trajectory information from dif­ ferent ships is treated as independent channels. Traditional recurrent architec­ tures such as LSTM, despite their widespread use in time-series modeling and demonstrated effectiveness in tasks like energy disaggregation through adaptive bidirectional variants [ 55 ], exhibit limited perfor­ mance in the complex, multi-vessel maritime environment, with ADE exceeding 1000m across all three datasets. The attention-augmented LSTM-based model ED-ATTN reduces ADE < 900m on CPW but yields an FDE surpassing 1000m on CJPW, revealing deficiencies in long-term dependency modeling. Moreover, SNIINet, the current state-of-the-art LSTM-based baseline, achieves an ADE on CPW that is 25.87% higher than that of KLDA-TICNet and incurs a longer inference time, primar­ ily due to its sequential processing nature, which restricts its ability to capture global ship interactions. Notably, KLDA-TICNet also surpasses the most recent methods, GATransformer and LMCA, by substantial margins: on the OPW dataset, it reduces ADE by 47.85% and 48.64% and FDE by 52.69% and 53.72%, respectively, highlighting its enhanced capability in modeling com­ plex multi-vessel interactions and long-term trajectory dynamics. These results highlight the effectiveness of the TICN module in modeling multi- ship interactions and the DSPE mechanism in optimizing heterogeneous feature decoupling and correlation modeling. Importantly, in terms of model parameter count and inference time, KLDA-TICNet achieves significant performance gains with only 1.02 million trainable parameters, far fewer than PatchTST and LMCA, demonstrating strong parameter efficiency. Its inference time of 1.82s is moderately higher, yet this added cost remains reasonable. In safety- critical maritime scenarios, the substantial gain in prediction accuracy more than offsets the slight latency increase, enhancing reliability for tasks like collision avoidance and route planning. Training time is another critical indicator of model efficiency and is closely related to the number of model parameters. Models with fewer parameters, such as GRU and LSTM, exhibit shorter training times, whereas parameter-heavy architectures like PatchTST and TCN- Transformer incur relatively longer training durations. The proposed KLDA-TICNet, with 1.02M parameters, requires 4.93s per epoch—a longer training time compared to most baselines. This increased compu­ tational cost primarily stems from its CTD cascade mechanism, which processes consecutive time steps in a non-parallelized manner dur­ ing prediction. It effectively captures spatiotemporal trajectory patterns enhancing predictive accuracy.

sections.heading: Analysis of Validation Consistency.
sections.text: Based on the trained model, this study validates the predictive consistency and generalization sta­ bility of the proposed model. The dataset was partitioned into training and test sets at an 8:2 ratio. The testing set was excluded from both model training and hyperparameter tuning. From the training set, a ran­ dom subset comprising 25% of its samples—equivalent to 20% of the full dataset—was selected to form an internal validation subset, which was used to assess the model’s predictive stability across different data subsamples. As shown in Table 5 , all evaluation metrics for both the internal validation set and the test set exhibit high consistency across differ­ ent water areas, with relative deviations ranging from 3% to 5.6%. This minor variation is attributed to random subsampling in the ab­ sence of systematic data distribution bias. These results confirm that the model demonstrates stable performance across diverse data sub­ sets, shows no signs of overfitting, and achieves reliable generalization capability. 4.3.2 . sections.heading: Discussion on the effectiveness of TICN.
sections.text: In TICN of DSPE, without transposition, using only temporal stream data for ship interaction leads to MAE increases of 24.07%, 11.11%, and 27.50% in three maritime scenarios. Conversely, using only transposition (feature stream) data re­ sults in MAE increases of 40.74%, 18.52%, and 72.50%. Dual-stream integration achieves at least 11.11% performance improvement over single-stream structures, enabling collaborative time-feature sequence modeling, as shown in Table 10 . This validates that transposed fea­ ture streams can independently represent heterogeneous features as tokens via self-attention, explicitly modeling feature correlations and mitigating attention ambiguity caused by feature coupling in traditional temporal streams. Notably, the full dual-stream model has 1.02M parameters and an inference time of 1.82s; in contrast, the temporal-stream-only variant has 0.66M parameters and takes 1.42s, while the transposed feature- stream-only variant has 0.69M parameters and takes 1.52s. Although the full model incurs only a slight increase in parameter count and inference latency over either single-stream counterpart, it achieves sub­ stantially better performance. Moreover, the introduction of sequence transposition increases training time from 2.59s in the ablated variants to 4.93s in the full model, but the transposition operation is crucial to the model enhanced performance. Together, these results demonstrate that the dual-stream architecture delivers meaningful gains in predictive capability with limited additional computational cost during inference, at the expense of moderately higher training overhead.

sections.heading: Discussion on the effectiveness of KLDA.
sections.text: In the proposed method, the attention mechanism is critical to model performance. To compare experiments with other attention mechanisms such as scaled-dot product attention (SDPA) and additive attention (AddA), Table 11 demonstrates that KLDA achieves 14.28% and over 20.58% improvements in trajec­ tory prediction accuracy compared to SDPA and AddA, respectively. Visual analysis in Fig. 12 reveals faster convergence and higher stability across three areas, with validation loss reaching the convergence thresh­ old in fewer iterations. The analysis indicates that KLDA suppresses local outliers in attention maps by mapping feature vectors to probabil­ ity distributions for similarity computation, thereby enhancing model robustness and generalization. KLDA-TICNet has nearly the same parameter count as SDPA-TICNet and AddA-TICNet, with only marginally higher inference time (1.82s vs. 1.66s and 1.68s, respectively) and slightly longer training time (4.93s vs. 4.64s and 4.71s, respectively). Despite this modest increase in computa­ tional overhead, KLDA-TICNet achieves substantially better prediction accuracy, demonstrating that KLDA delivers significant performance gains at minimal additional computational cost.

sections.heading: Discussion on the effectiveness of CTD.
sections.text: While the model demon­ strates superior predictive performance, its computational overhead and capability in modeling navigational uncertainty warrant systematic eval­ uation. The results from the multi-horizon prediction experiments across three maritime regions are reported in Table 12 , focusing on two key aspects: inference efficiency and robustness to uncertainty. Robustness and navigational uncertainty: Maritime vessel behavior is influenced by complex factors such as human decision-making, render­ ing uncertainty modeling highly challenging. The results of Tables 12 and 9 show that the CTD-enhanced model exhibits consistently stable performance across all three waterways. MAE, ADE, and FDE increase smoothly with prediction sequence length. The cascaded decoding ar­ chitecture effectively captures spatiotemporal trajectory patterns and suppresses the effects of uncertainty. Although the error has increased, the error growth remains smooth and controllable, and there has been no abrupt degradation, reflecting the model’s good robustness and generalization ability in the face of navigation uncertainty.
